analysis.one_liner: Requires employers to protect workers from dangerous heat with water, shade, paid rest breaks, and cooling measures.
analysis.headline: The House labor committee approved the bill 27–19 and reported it on November 7, 2022, with 116 cosponsors, but it never received a House floor vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have directed OSHA to write, within a year, the first national standard protecting workers from heat stress. Employers who couldn't engineer the heat away would have to provide drinking water, shade or cool-down spaces, acclimatization policies, and periodic paid rest breaks, plus training in the signs of heat illness, with whistleblower protection for workers who complain. It is named for Asunción Valdivia, a California farmworker who died of heat stroke in 2004 after a long day picking grapes in extreme heat. The House labor committee approved it and put it on the House calendar, but no floor vote ever happened.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers in hot jobs — farmworkers, construction crews, warehouse and delivery workers, kitchen staff — would gain enforceable rights to water, shade, paid rest breaks, and training in heat illness, with protection from retaliation for reporting problems. Heat is one of the deadliest weather hazards for outdoor workers, and farmworkers in particular often lack these basics.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Farm, construction, warehouse, and delivery workers

how_it_helps.text: Directs OSHA to issue an interim final heat-protection standard within one year, requiring employers to either engineer heat away or provide employer-paid hydration, periodic paid rest breaks, access to shade or cool-down spaces, and acclimatization policies [S3][S4].
Requires that mandated rest breaks, medical removal, and training time be paid at the employee's regular rate, so workers don't lose wages for taking safety breaks [S4].
Requires training, posters, and plans in English and in a language the workers understand, aimed at the heavily immigrant workforce most exposed to heat [S4].

Extends whistleblower protection and a four-year window for issuing citations, and adds heat-illness questions to the National Agricultural Workers Survey so farmworker heat injuries are actually counted [S3][S4].

analysis.who_pays: Employers in heat-exposed industries — agriculture, construction, warehousing, delivery, and food service — would bear the cost of water, shade or cooling equipment, acclimatization scheduling, training, and paid rest breaks that reduce productive work time during hot hours.
analysis.who_pays_short: Heat-exposed employers, especially farms and contractors

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs fall directly on employers in thin-margin industries: buying shade structures or cooling equipment, restructuring schedules, and paying for rest breaks that take crews off task during the hottest, most productive hours [S4].

The bill fast-tracks rulemaking: the first standard would be an interim final rule issued without the normal advance notice-and-comment process, the Paperwork Reduction Act, or environmental review, and courts are directed to defer to the Labor Secretary's reasonable interpretations [S4] — critics would call this rushed regulation with little chance to challenge it before it takes effect.

The standard's details are left largely to the Secretary of Labor's judgment rather than spelled out in the bill, so the practical burden on any given employer would depend on how the rule is written [S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protections are basic and well tested — California and other states have enforced similar heat rules for years, and the bill treats any proven state-plan requirement as presumptively feasible [S4]. The cost is real compliance spending by heat-exposed employers, but it buys directly fewer heat strokes and deaths among some of the lowest-paid workers in the country. The main honest objection is procedural: issuing the first rule without the normal comment period limits the chance to tailor it to unusual workplaces.

outcome.mechanism: The House labor committee approved it 27–19 and reported it on November 7, 2022, placing it on the Union Calendar, but House leadership never brought it to the floor for a vote, and it died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

narrative.text: Introduced on March 26, 2021 and referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor, where it sat for over a year [S6].
The committee held a markup on July 27, 2022 and ordered the bill reported as amended by a vote of 27–19 [S6].

The committee reported the amended bill on November 7, 2022 (H. Rept. 117-547) and it was placed on the Union Calendar, Calendar No. 393, meaning it was eligible for House floor consideration [S4][S6].
No further action appears in the record — no floor debate, no vote, no Senate action — and the Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S6].
The bill had 116 cosponsors, all of them Democrats [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers in heat-exposed industries — agriculture, construction, warehousing, delivery — avoided the compliance costs of mandated water, shade, cooling, and paid rest breaks. Heat-exposed workers gained no federal protection, since no standalone heat standard was enacted in that Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Heat-exposed employers who avoided compliance costs

sides.party_line_note: All 116 cosponsors were Democrats and the committee vote to advance the bill was 27–19; the bill cleared committee but the Democratic-run House never voted on it.

industries.note: Farmworkers are among the workers most likely to die of heat, and the bill would have required water, shade, acclimatization scheduling, and paid rest breaks, plus new survey tracking of farmworker heat illness. Growers and labor contractors would bear those costs, which fall hardest during the hottest harvest hours.
Outdoor construction crews in hot weather would have gained mandated hydration, cool-down space, and paid breaks; contractors would bear the cost in equipment and lost work time.

industries.industry: Warehousing, delivery, and other hot indoor work
industries.note: The standard covers indoor heat too, so warehouses and kitchens without climate control would have faced cooling or rest-break requirements and their associated costs.
